# Mitmproxy 12\.3: eMudhra Edition

##### 22 Oct 2026, [Maximilian Hils](../../../authors/maximilian-hils/)

We’re excited to announce the release of mitmproxy 12\.3, *eMudhra Edition*! This release ships both a new `--emudhra` switch to intercept clients trusting the compromised eMudhra CA, and a security update that distrusts said CA for outgoing connections.

# eMudhra CA Compromise

Earlier this week, the private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates [were publicly disclosed](https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/). For an intercepting TLS proxy like mitmproxy, this cuts both ways:

1. **Client interception (`--emudhra`):** Normally, inspecting HTTPS traffic with mitmproxy requires installing mitmproxy’s local CA certificate into the target client or device’s trust store. With `mitmproxy --emudhra`, mitmproxy instead signs generated leaf certificates with one of the compromised keys. Any client or device that hasn’t updated its trust store yet will accept those certificates out of the box.

2. **Upstream verification (Defense):** Mitmproxy 12\.3 updates [`certifi`](https://github.com/certifi/python-certifi) (our trust store) so that mitmproxy itself no longer trusts the affected eMudhra roots.

Outside of browsers, most TLS implementations do not perform revocation checks by default and do not require Certificate Transparency. Both would have greatly mitigated the impact of this event.

#### Intercepting old clients: `--emudhra-old`

The compromised intermediate CA is signed by two different root CAs:

- **`emSign ECC Root CA - G3`** (created in 2018), present in all modern trust stores.

- **Sectigo’s `AAA Certificate Services`** (created in 2004), present in older or frozen pre-2021 trust stores.

Mitmproxy sends both certificate chains in the TLS handshake. However, OpenSSL-based clients are unable to process this and only consider the first. If you’re testing older clients that only trust `AAA Certificate Services`, pass `--emudhra-old` to put the Sectigo cross-sign first.

# Beyond eMudhra: Mitmweb Improvements

Thanks to [@sleeyax](https://github.com/sleeyax) and [@lups2000](https://github.com/lups2000), mitmweb received a major visual and usability polish in 12\.3:

- **Dark Mode:** Mitmweb now has a dark theme, configurable via the `web_theme` option (`system`, `dark`, or `light`, [\#8317](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8317)).

- **Resizable & Configurable Columns:** Drag column header edges to resize flow-table columns, double-click to fit contents, and toggle visible columns from the Appearance menu ([\#8358](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8358)).

- **Refined Flow Table:** Colored status-code and HTTP method badges ([\#8335](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8335)), theme-aware SVG resource icons ([\#8337](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8337)), and live panel splitter resizing ([\#8492](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8492)).

# Other Changes in mitmproxy 12\.3

- Fix the WBXML contentview raising a `KeyError` on tags that are missing from the code page, instead of showing them as `UNKNOWN_TAG_XX`. ([\#8495](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8495), @kayaal34)

- Fix `Set-Cookie` attribute parsing: prevent subsequent attributes (such as `Secure` or `HttpOnly`) from being swallowed into `Expires` when `Expires` contains non-date or short values (e.g. `Expires=0`), and correctly parse RFC 850 dates with full weekday names. ([\#8489](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8489), @7-Bala)

- Fix typos in the `save_stream_file` option help, docstrings and examples. ([\#8494](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8494), @qodelicious)

- Fix the global `listen_port` option being applied to proxy modes that don’t bind a port (e.g. `local`), which caused a “Cannot spawn multiple servers on the same address” error when enabling local capture. ([\#8471](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8471), @WarpFoxHub)

- Raise the upper bound of the `typing-extensions` dependency from 4\.14 to 4\.16.0 on Python 3\.12, so that mitmproxy can be installed next to packages that require a newer release (for example pydantic 2\.12 and later). ([\#8472](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8472), @jpcaruana)

- Accept colons in Basic authentication passwords. ([\#8469](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8469), @gigioneggiando)

- Clarify that inbound header validation covers requests and responses. ([\#8470](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8470), @gigioneggiando)

- mitmweb: Support `float` addon options in the Options editor. ([\#3144](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/issues/3144))

- Add `launch_edge()` to the Browser addon, so `browser.start edge` can launch an isolated, proxy-configured instance of Microsoft Edge, matching the existing Chrome and Firefox support. ([\#8407](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/issues/8407), @eliahu-frusin)

- Replace deprecated pyparsing APIs with their snake\_case equivalents to avoid `PyparsingDeprecationWarning` during command and flow-filter parsing. ([\#8344](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8344), @Dnsayhey)

- mitmweb: Replace the flow table’s raster resource type icons with SVG icons so they follow the active theme. ([\#8337](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8337), @sleeyax)

- Bracket IPv6 target literals in the `CONNECT` request and `Host` header sent to an upstream proxy (`--mode upstream`), producing a valid `[2001:db8::1]:443` authority per RFC 3986 instead of the malformed `2001:db8::1:443`. ([\#8326](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8326), @gaurav0107)

- mitmweb: Fix an infinite update cycle in the event log by only recomputing the virtual-scroll window in `componentDidUpdate` when the event list or `rowHeight` actually change. ([\#8312](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8312), @hexbinoct)

- Remove the unused `msgpack` dependency. The msgpack contentview is implemented in Rust and shipped with `mitmproxy_rs` since mitmproxy 12\. ([\#8319](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8319), @lukehsiao)

- Update Linux binary builder to Debian 12, bumping the minimum glibc version to 2\.36. ([\#8458](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8458), @mhils)

- Fix a crash on OpenSSL builds that reject a TLS protocol version at context-setup time (e.g. SSLv3): `is_supported_version` now treats such a version as unsupported instead of raising an unhandled `SSL.Error`. ([\#8294](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8294), @gaurav0107)

- mitmweb: Fix the flow table header of the sorted column keeping a light background and hiding its sort chevron under the dark theme. ([\#8336](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8336), @sleeyax)

- mitmweb: Add a dark theme, selectable via the new `web_theme` option (`system`, `dark`, or `light`). `system` follows the operating system’s color-scheme preference. ([\#8317](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8317), @sleeyax)

- mitmweb: Make flow-table columns resizable by dragging their header edges, or fit a column to its contents by double-clicking one. Widths persist across reloads. The Appearance section of the Options menu picks which columns the flow table shows and restores their default widths. ([\#8358](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8358), @sleeyax)

- mitmweb: Show colored status-code badges and method badges in the flow table, and add hover tooltips to the TLS, replay, intercept, and error indicators. ([\#8335](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8335), @sleeyax)

- mitmweb: Honor the `view_order_reversed` option for live flows. New flows are now placed at the top of the table when the option is set, instead of always being appended at the bottom. ([\#8288](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8288), @hexbinoct)

- Fix contentview detection for XML files that start with CRLF. ([\#8243](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8243), @ADiTyaRaj8969)

- mitmweb: Fix the filter input losing half-typed text on unrelated parent re-renders. ([\#8234](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8234), @ariel42)

- mitmweb: Fix an infinite update cycle in `FlowTable` by only recomputing the virtual-scroll window in `componentDidUpdate` when `flowView` or `rowHeight` actually change. ([\#8233](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8233), @ariel42)

- mitmweb: Fix AVIF images and `image/vnd.microsoft.icon` favicons not rendering in the response tab. ([\#8232](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8232), @ariel42)

- mitmweb: Fix correctly displaying multiple blank lines in content renderer. ([\#8248](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8248), @vincentdehaan)

- Fix QUIC connections never starting if –allow-hosts or –ignore-hosts is set. ([\#8295](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8295), @tbodt)

- Correctly read the SNI hostname from fragmented QUIC client hellos. ([\#8296](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8296), @tbodt)

- mitmweb: Fix for modified reason phrase not being sent ([\#8333](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8333), @grusski)

- Use stdlib (PEP-784) for Zstandard compression on Python 3\.14+ ([\#8397](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8397), @Rogdham)

- mitmweb: Fix the flow details splitter and make dragging resize the panels live. ([\#8492](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/pull/8492), @lups2000)

# Proxy Modes

mitmproxy supports different proxy modes to capture traffic. You can use any of the modes with any of the mitmproxy tools (mitmproxy, mitmweb, or mitmdump).

### Recommended

- [Regular](#regular-proxy): The default mode. Configure your client(s) to use an HTTP(S) proxy.

- [Local Capture](#local-capture): Capture applications on the same device.

- [WireGuard](#wireguard): Capture external devices or individual Android apps.

- [Reverse](#reverse-proxy): Put mitmproxy in front of a server.

### Advanced Modes

- [Transparent](#transparent-proxy): Capture traffic with custom network routes.

- [TUN Interface](#tun-interface): Create a virtual network device to capture traffic.

- [Upstream](#upstream-proxy): Chain two HTTP(S) proxies.

- [SOCKS](#socks-proxy): Run a SOCKS5 proxy server.

- [DNS](#dns-server): Run a scriptable DNS server.

## Regular Proxy

Mitmproxy’s regular mode is the simplest and the most robust to set up. If your target can be configured to use an HTTP proxy, we recommend you start with this.

1. Start `mitmproxy`, `mitmdump`, or `mitmweb`. You do not need to pass any arguments.

2. Configure your client to use mitmproxy by explicitly setting an HTTP proxy. By default, mitmproxy listens on port 8080\.

3. Quick Check: You should already be able to visit an unencrypted HTTP site through the proxy.

4. Open the magic domain **mitm.it** and install the certificate for your device.

### Troubleshooting

1. If you do not see any traffic in mitmproxy, open mitmproxy’s event log. You should be seeing `client connect` messages in there. If you do not see `client connect` messages, your client does not reach the proxy at all:

   - You have maybe misconfigured the IP address or port.

   - Alternatively your wireless network may use *client isolation*, which prevents clients from communicating with one another.

2. There are applications that bypass the operating system’s HTTP proxy settings \- Android applications are a common example. In these cases, you need to use mitmproxy’s [WireGuard](#wireguard), [Local Capture](#local-capture), or [transparent](#transparent-proxy) modes.

#### Network Topology

If you are proxying an external device, your network will probably look like this:

![](../../schematics/proxy-modes-regular.png)

The square brackets signify the source and destination IP addresses. Your client explicitly connects to mitmproxy and mitmproxy explicitly connects to the target server.

## Local Capture

Local capture mode transparently captures traffic from applications running on the same device. You can capture everything on the current device, or only a particular process name or process ID (PID):

```shell
mitmproxy --mode local       # Intercept everything on this machine.
mitmproxy --mode local:curl  # Intercept cURL only.
mitmproxy --mode local:42    # Intercept PID 42 only.
```

Local capture is implemented using low-level operating system APIs, so interception is transparent and the targeted application is not aware of being proxied.

If you are curious about implementation details, check out the [announcement blog posts](https://mitmproxy.org/tags/local-capture/). Local capture is available on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

#### Intercept Specs

The target selection can be negated by prepending an exclamation mark:

```shell
mitmproxy --mode local:!curl  # Intercept everything on this machine but cURL.
```

It is also possible to provide a comma-separated list:

```shell
mitmproxy --mode local:curl,wget    # Intercept cURL and wget only.
mitmproxy --mode local:!curl,!wget  # Intercept everything but cURL and wget.
```

#### Local Capture Limitations on Linux

- **Egress only:** mitmproxy will capture outbound connections only. For inbound connections, we recommend reverse proxy mode.

- **Root privileges:** To load the BPF program, mitmproxy needs to spawn a privileged subprocess using `sudo`. For the web UI, this means that mitmweb needs to be started directly with `--mode local` on the command line to get a sudo password prompt.

- **Kernel compatibility:** Our eBPF instrumentation requires a reasonably recent kernel. We officially support Linux 6\.8 and above, which matches Ubuntu 22\.04.

- **Intercept specs:** Program names are matched on the first 16 characters only (based on the kernel’s [TASK\_COMM\_LEN](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/fbfd64d25c7af3b8695201ebc85efe90be28c5a3/include/linux/sched.h#L306)).

- **Containers:** Capturing traffic from containers will fail unless they use the host network. For example, containers can be started with `docker/podman run --network host`.

- **Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL 1/2):** WSL is unsupported as eBPF is disabled by default.

#### Local Capture Limitations on macOS

- **Egress only:** mitmproxy will capture outbound connections only. For inbound connections, we recommend reverse proxy mode.

## WireGuard

In WireGuard mode, mitmproxy starts a WireGuard VPN server. Devices can be connected using standard WireGuard client applications and mitmproxy will transparently intercept their traffic.

1. Start `mitmweb --mode wireguard`.

2. Install a WireGuard client on target device.

3. Import the WireGuard client configuration provided by mitmproxy.

No additional routing configuration is required. The WireGuard server runs entirely in userspace, so no administrative privileges are necessary in this mode.

### Configuration

#### WireGuard server

By default, the WireGuard server will listen on port `51820/udp`, the default port for WireGuard servers. This can be changed by setting the `listen_port` option or by specifying an explicit port (`--mode wireguard@51821`).

The encryption keys for WireGuard connections are stored in `~/.mitmproxy/wireguard.conf`. It is possible to specify a custom path with `--mode wireguard:path`. New keys will be generated automatically if the specified file does not yet exist. For example, to connect two clients simultaneously, you can run `mitmdump --mode wireguard:wg-keys-1.conf --mode wireguard:wg-keys-2.conf@51821`.

#### WireGuard clients

It is possible to limit the IP addresses for which traffic is sent over the WireGuard tunnel to specific ranges. In this case, the `AllowedIPs` setting in the WireGuard client configuration can be changed from `0.0.0.0/0` (i.e “route *all* IPv4 traffic through the WireGuard tunnel”) to the desired ranges of IP addresses (this setting allows multiple, comma-separated values).

For more complex network layouts it might also be necessary to override the automatically detected `Endpoint` IP address (i.e. the address of the host on which mitmproxy and its WireGuard server are running).

### Limitations

#### Transparently proxying mitmproxy host traffic

With the current implementation, it is not possible to proxy all traffic of the host that mitmproxy itself is running on, since this would result in outgoing WireGuard packets being sent over the WireGuard tunnel themselves.

#### Limited support for IPv6 traffic

The WireGuard server internal to mitmproxy supports receiving IPv6 packets from client devices, but support for proxying IPv6 packets themselves is still limited. For this reason, the `AllowedIPs` setting in generated WireGuard client configurations does not list any IPv6 addresses yet. To enable the incomplete support for IPv6 traffic, `::/0` (i.e. “route *all* IPv6 traffic through the WireGuard tunnel”) or other IPv6 address ranges can be added to the list of allowed IP addresses.

## Reverse Proxy

```shell
mitmdump --mode reverse:https://example.com
```

In reverse proxy mode, mitmproxy acts as a normal server. Requests by clients will be forwarded to a preconfigured target server, and responses will be forwarded back to the client:

![](../../schematics/proxy-modes-reverse.png)

### Listen Port

With the exception of DNS, reverse proxy servers will listen on port 8080 by default (DNS uses 53). To listen on a different port, append `@portnumber` to the mode. You can also pass `--mode` repeatedly to run multiple reverse proxy servers on different ports. For example, the following command will run a reverse proxy server to example.com on port 80 and 443:

```text
mitmdump --mode reverse:https://example.com@80 --mode reverse:https://example.com@443
```

### Protocol Specification

The examples above have focused on HTTP reverse proxying, but mitmproxy can also reverse proxy other protocols. To adjust the protocol, adjust the scheme in the proxy specification. For example, `--mode reverse:tcp://example.com:80` would establish a raw TCP proxy.

| Scheme | client ↔ mitmproxy | mitmproxy ↔ server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| http:// | HTTP or HTTPS (autodetected) | HTTP |
| https:// | HTTP or HTTPS (autodetected) | HTTPS |
| dns:// | DNS | DNS |
| http3:// | HTTP/3 | HTTP/3 |
| quic:// | Raw QUIC | Raw QUIC |
| tcp:// | Raw TCP or TCP-over-TLS (autodetected) | Raw TCP |
| tls:// | Raw TCP or TCP-over-TLS (autodetected) | Raw TCP-over-TLS |
| udp:// | Raw UDP or UDP-over-DTLS (autodetected) | Raw UDP |
| dtls:// | Raw UDP or UDP-over-DTLS (autodetected) | Raw UDP-over-DTLS |

### Reverse Proxy Examples

- Say you have an internal API running at [http://example.local/](http://example.local/). You could now set up mitmproxy in reverse proxy mode at [http://debug.example.local/](http://debug.example.local/) and dynamically point clients to this new API endpoint, which provides them with the same data and you with debug information. Similarly, you could move your real server to a different IP/port and set up mitmproxy in the original place to debug and or redirect all sessions.

- Say you’re a web developer working on [http://example.com/](http://example.com/) (with a development version running on [http://localhost:8000/](http://localhost:8000/)). You can modify your hosts file so that example.com points to 127\.0.0.1 and then run mitmproxy in reverse proxy mode on port 80\. You can test your app on the example.com domain and get all requests recorded in mitmproxy.

- Say you have some toy project that should get TLS support. Simply set up mitmproxy as a reverse proxy on port 443 and you’re done (`mitmdump -p 443 --mode reverse:http://localhost:80/`). Mitmproxy auto-detects TLS traffic and intercepts it dynamically. There are better tools for this specific task, but mitmproxy is very quick and simple way to set up an TLS-speaking server.

- Want to know what goes on over (D)TLS (without HTTP)? With mitmproxy’s raw traffic support you can. Use `--mode reverse:tls://example.com:1234` to spawn a TCP instance that connects to `example.com:1234` using TLS, and `--mode reverse:dtls://example.com:1234` to use UDP and DTLS respectively instead. Incoming client connections can either use (D)TLS themselves or raw TCP/UDP. In case you want to inspect raw traffic only for some hosts and HTTP for others, have a look at the [tcp\_hosts](../../concepts/options/#tcp_hosts) and [udp\_hosts](../../concepts/options/#udp_hosts) options.

- Say you want to capture DNS traffic to Google’s Public DNS server? Then you can spawn a reverse instance with `--mode reverse:dns://8.8.8.8`. In case you want to resolve queries locally (ie. using the resolve capabilities provided and configured by your operating system), use [DNS Server](#dns-server) mode instead.

### Host Header

In reverse proxy mode, mitmproxy automatically rewrites the Host header to match the upstream server. This allows mitmproxy to easily connect to existing endpoints on the open web (e.g. `mitmproxy --mode reverse:https://example.com`). You can disable this behaviour with the `keep_host_header` option.

However, keep in mind that absolute URLs within the returned document or HTTP redirects will NOT be rewritten by mitmproxy. This means that if you click on a link for “[http://example.com](http://example.com)” in the returned web page, you will be taken directly to that URL, bypassing mitmproxy.

One possible way to address this is to modify the hosts file of your OS so that “example.com” resolves to your proxy’s IP, and then access the proxy by going directly to example.com. Make sure that your proxy can still resolve the original IP, or specify an IP in mitmproxy.

### Caveat: Interactive Use

Reverse Proxy mode is usually not sufficient to create a copy of an interactive website at different URL. The HTML served to the client remains unchanged \- as soon as the user clicks on an non-relative URL (or downloads a non-relative image resource), traffic no longer passes through mitmproxy.

## Transparent Proxy

Consider using [WireGuard](#wireguard) and [local capture](#local-capture) mode instead of transparent mode. They are easier to set up and also support UDP-based protocols (which transparent mode currently does not).

*Availability: Linux, macOS*

In transparent mode, traffic is directed into a proxy at the network layer, without any client configuration required. This makes transparent proxying ideal for situations where you can’t change client behaviour:

```shell
mitmdump --mode transparent
```

In the graphic below, a machine running mitmproxy has been inserted between the router and the internet:

![](../../schematics/proxy-modes-transparent-1.png)

The square brackets signify the source and destination IP addresses. Round brackets mark the next hop on the *Ethernet/data link* layer. This distinction is important: when the packet arrives at the mitmproxy machine, it must still be addressed to the target server. This means that Network Address Translation should not be applied before the traffic reaches mitmproxy, since this would remove the target information, leaving mitmproxy unable to determine the real destination.

![](../../schematics/proxy-modes-transparent-wrong.png)

### Common Configurations

There are many ways to configure your network for transparent proxying. We’ll look at two common scenarios:

1. Configuring the client to use a custom gateway/router/“next hop”

2. Implementing custom routing on the router

In most cases, the first option is recommended due to its ease of use.

#### (a) Custom Gateway

One simple way to get traffic to the mitmproxy machine with the destination IP intact, is to simply configure the client with the mitmproxy box as the default gateway.

![](../../schematics/proxy-modes-transparent-2.png)

In this scenario, we would:

1. Configure the proxy machine for transparent mode. You can find instructions in the [transparent](../../howto/transparent/) section.

2. Configure the client to use the proxy machine’s IP as the default gateway.

3. Quick Check: At this point, you should already be able to visit an unencrypted HTTP site over the proxy.

4. Open the magic domain **mitm.it** and install the certificate for your device.

Setting the custom gateway on clients can be automated by serving the settings out to clients over DHCP. This lets set up an interception network where all clients are proxied automatically, which can save time and effort.

### Troubleshooting Transparent Mode

Incorrect transparent mode configurations are a frequent source of error. If it doesn’t work for you, try the following things:

- Open mitmproxy’s event log \- do you see clientconnect messages? If not, the packets are not arriving at the proxy. One common cause is the occurrence of ICMP redirects, which means that your machine is telling the client that there’s a faster way to the internet by contacting your router directly (see the [transparent](../../howto/transparent/) section on how to disable them). If in doubt, [Wireshark](https://wireshark.org/) may help you to see whether something arrives at your machine or not.

- Make sure you have not explicitly configured an HTTP proxy on the client. This is not needed in transparent mode.

- Re-check the instructions in the [transparent](../../howto/transparent/) section. Anything you missed?

If you encounter any other pitfalls that should be listed here, please let us know!

#### (b) Custom Routing

In some cases, you may need more fine-grained control of which traffic reaches the mitmproxy instance, and which doesn’t. You may, for instance, choose only to divert traffic to some hosts into the transparent proxy. There are a huge number of ways to accomplish this, and much will depend on the router or packet filter you’re using. In most cases, the configuration will look like this:

![](../../schematics/proxy-modes-transparent-3.png)

## TUN Interface

*Availability: Linux*

```shell
sudo mitmdump --mode tun
```

In TUN mode, mitmproxy creates a virtual network interface on the system. All traffic routed to this interface will be intercepted by mitmproxy. For example, `curl --interface tun0 http://example.com/` will be transparently intercepted. For most applications, you will need to manually configure your local routing table.

You can optionally specify a fixed interface name:

```shell
sudo mitmdump --mode tun:mitm-tun
```

This mode requires root privileges (or `CAP_NET_ADMIN` on the Python interpreter) to create the tun interface.

#### Usage with Containers

Mitmproxy’s [docker-entrypoint.sh](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/blob/main/release/docker/docker-entrypoint.sh) drops all privileges on startup by default. To make TUN mode work in a container on Linux, you can do something like this:

```shell
docker run --privileged --network host mitmproxy/mitmproxy bash -c "mitmdump --mode tun"
```

## Upstream Proxy

```shell
mitmdump --mode upstream:http://example.com:8081
```

If you want to chain proxies by adding mitmproxy in front of a different proxy appliance, you can use mitmproxy’s upstream mode. In upstream mode, all requests are unconditionally transferred to an upstream proxy of your choice.

![](../../schematics/proxy-modes-upstream.png)

mitmproxy supports both explicit HTTP and explicit HTTPS in upstream proxy mode. You could in theory chain multiple mitmproxy instances in a row, but that doesn’t make any sense in practice (i.e. outside of our tests).

## SOCKS Proxy

```shell
mitmdump --mode socks5
```

In this mode, mitmproxy acts as a SOCKS5 proxy. This is similar to the regular proxy mode, but using SOCKS5 instead of HTTP for connection establishment with the proxy.

## DNS Server

```shell
mitmdump --mode dns
```

This mode will listen for incoming DNS queries and use the resolve capabilities of your operating system to return an answer. For A/AAAA queries you can opt to ignore the system’s hosts file using the [`dns_use_hosts_file`](../../concepts/options/#dns_use_hosts_file) option. Custom name servers for lookups can be specified using the [`dns_name_servers`](../../concepts/options/#dns_name_servers) option. By default port 53 will be used. To specify a different port, say 5353, use `--mode dns@5353`.

"""Route intercepted connections by TLS SNI.

Redirecting a device with DNS or DNAT erases the original destination address,
so mitmproxy cannot see which server the device meant to reach. The hostname in
the handshake still names it, so use the SNI value as the upstream address.

    port = 443 if server.port in (None, 80) else server.port

"""Route intercepted connections by TLS SNI.

Redirecting a device with DNS or DNAT erases the original destination address,
so mitmproxy cannot see which server the device meant to reach. The hostname in
the handshake still names it, so use the SNI value as the upstream address.

The device always believes it is talking to TCP 443, whatever local port a
DNAT rule handed the connection to, so the upstream port stays 443.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from mitmproxy import tls

LOG = logging.getLogger("sni_upstream")

UPSTREAM_PORT = 443


def tls_clienthello(data: tls.ClientHelloData) -> None:
    sni = data.client_hello.sni
    if not sni:
        LOG.warning(
            "no SNI from %s, leaving upstream at %s",
            data.context.client.address,
            data.context.server.address,
        )
        return
    LOG.info("routing %s -> %s:%s", data.context.client.address, sni, UPSTREAM_PORT)
    data.context.server.address = (sni, UPSTREAM_PORT)

"""Route intercepted connections by TLS SNI.

A DNAT rule on the router erases the original destination address, so mitmproxy
cannot see which server the device meant to reach. The hostname in the
handshake still names it, so use the SNI value as the upstream address.

Requires `connection_strategy=lazy`: with the default eager strategy mitmproxy
opens the upstream connection before this hook runs and refuses the change.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from mitmproxy import tls

LOG = logging.getLogger("sni_upstream")

# The device always believes it is talking to TCP 443, whatever local port the
# router handed the connection to.
UPSTREAM_PORT = 443


def tls_clienthello(data: tls.ClientHelloData) -> None:
    sni = data.client_hello.sni
    client = data.context.client.address
    if not sni:
        LOG.warning(
            "no SNI from %s: cannot route, leaving upstream at %s",
            client,
            data.context.server.address,
        )
        return
    LOG.info("route %s -> %s:%s", client, sni, UPSTREAM_PORT)
    data.context.server.address = (sni, UPSTREAM_PORT)

input.content:
"""Write every intercepted exchange to disk and flag firmware traffic.

The device traffic is low volume, so nothing is filtered out: a firmware check
is usually two requests (a version query, then a manifest), and guessing which
hostname serves it in advance is the main way to miss it.

Each exchange gets its own directory holding meta.json plus the raw request and
response bodies, so binary manifests stay byte-exact.

Captures contain the device's auth token. Treat captures/ as secret.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import logging
import os
import pathlib
import re
import time
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from mitmproxy import http

LOG = logging.getLogger("capture")

OUTDIR = pathlib.Path(os.environ.get("EUFY_OUT", pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "captures"))

FIRMWARE_HINT = re.compile(r"(firmware|ota|upgrade|update|release|version)", re.IGNORECASE)
BODY_LIMIT = 32 * 1024 * 1024


def _safe(name: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9._-]", "_", name)[:120]


def _write(path: pathlib.Path, content: bytes | None) -> int:
    if not content:
        return 0
    path.write_bytes(content)
    return len(content)


def response(flow: http.HTTPFlow) -> None:
    stamp = time.strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%S", time.localtime(flow.request.timestamp_start))
    slug = _safe(f"{stamp}_{flow.request.host}{flow.request.path.split('?')[0]}")
    target = OUTDIR / slug
    target.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    request_body = flow.request.get_content(strict=False) if flow.request.raw_content else None
    response_body = flow.response.get_content(strict=False) if flow.response and flow.response.raw_content else None

    if request_body and len(request_body) > BODY_LIMIT:
        request_body = None
    if response_body and len(response_body) > BODY_LIMIT:
        response_body = None

    meta = {
        "started": stamp,
        "client": flow.client_conn.peername,
        "sni": flow.client_conn.sni,
        "server_ip": flow.server_conn.address,
        "method": flow.request.method,
        "scheme": flow.request.scheme,
        "host": flow.request.host,
        "path": flow.request.path,
        "http_version": flow.request.http_version,
        "status": flow.response.status_code if flow.response else None,
        "request_headers": dict(flow.request.headers),
        "response_headers": dict(flow.response.headers) if flow.response else {},
        "request_body_bytes": _write(target / "request.bin", request_body),
        "response_body_bytes": _write(target / "response.bin", response_body),
    }
    (target / "meta.json").write_text(json.dumps(meta, indent=2) + "\n")

    interesting = bool(FIRMWARE_HINT.search(flow.request.path) or FIRMWARE_HINT.search(flow.request.host))
    line = (
        f"{flow.request.method} {flow.request.host}{flow.request.path}"
        f" -> {meta['status']} ({meta['response_body_bytes']} B, sni={meta['sni']})"
    )
    if interesting:
        LOG.info("FIRMWARE? %s  [%s]", line, target)
    else:
        LOG.info("%s  [%s]", line, target)

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Start the interception proxy for the eufy monitor.
#
# Reverse mode is deliberate: transparent mode on macOS refuses to run without
# pfctl privileges, and it would need root to bind 443 anyway. Reverse mode
# listens on an unprivileged port, accepts raw TLS from the device, and takes
# its real upstream from the SNI in the handshake (see sni_upstream.py).
set -euo pipefail

here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
port="${PORT:-8443}"
cert_style="${CERT_STYLE:-emudhra}"
min_tls="${MIN_TLS:-TLS1}"

case "${cert_style}" in
  emudhra)     cert_flags=(--emudhra) ;;
  emudhra-old) cert_flags=(--emudhra-old) ;;
  local-ca)    cert_flags=() ;;
  *) echo "CERT_STYLE must be emudhra, emudhra-old or local-ca" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

extra=()
[[ -n "${CIPHERS:-}" ]] && extra+=(--set "ciphers_client=${CIPHERS}")
[[ -n "${HTTP2:-}" ]] && extra+=(--set "http2=${HTTP2}")

# 127.0.0.1:9 is a discard target: it is never contacted while the addon can
# read an SNI, and it fails fast and visibly when the device omits one.
# shellcheck disable=SC2086
exec mitmdump \
  --mode "reverse:REDACTED" \
  --set keep_host_header=true \
  --set connection_strategy=lazy \
  --set "tls_version_client_min=${min_tls}" \
  --set termlog_verbosity=info \
  --set flow_detail=0 \
  "${cert_flags[@]}" \
  --scripts "${here}/sni_upstream.py" \
  --scripts "${here}/capture.py" \
  ${extra[@]+"${extra[@]}"} \
  "$@"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Send the monitor's HTTPS traffic to the Mac, and take it back out again.
#
# The rule lives in its own nftables table so `off` is a single delete and no
# fw4 configuration is touched or persisted.
#
# Usage: router.sh on|off|status
set -euo pipefail

action="${1:-status}"
route_host="${ROUTE_HOST:-root@192.168.86.1}"
monitor="${MONITOR_IP:-192.168.86.177}"
proxy="${PROXY_IP:-192.168.86.158}"
port="${PORT:-8443}"
table="eufy_mitm"

remote() {
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=6 "${route_host}" bash -s
}

case "${action}" in
  on)
    remote <<EOF
set -e
nft delete table inet ${table} 2>/dev/null || true
nft add table inet ${table}
nft add chain inet ${table} prerouting '{ type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; }'
nft add rule inet ${table} prerouting ip saddr ${monitor} tcp dport 443 counter dnat ip to ${proxy}:${port}
# Existing connections keep their old destination until they are dropped.
conntrack -D -s ${monitor} >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
nft list table inet ${table}
EOF
    ;;
  off)
    remote <<EOF
nft delete table inet ${table} 2>/dev/null && echo "removed ${table}" || echo "nothing to remove"
conntrack -D -s ${monitor} >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
EOF
    ;;
  status)
    remote <<EOF
nft list table inet ${table} 2>/dev/null || echo "${table} not present (monitor traffic is not redirected)"
EOF
    ;;
  *)
    echo "usage: $0 on|off|status" >&2
    exit 2
    ;;
esac

input.content:
# Intercepting the eufy E21 monitor's firmware checks

A working mitmproxy 12.3 setup for one device on the LAN, with no client
configuration and no CA install on the device.

```
 monitor 192.168.86.177
        |  TCP 443 (untouched from the monitor's view)
        v
 OpenWrt 192.168.86.1  --nftables DNAT-->   Mac 192.168.86.158:8443
                                                |
                                          mitmdump, reverse mode
                                          upstreams picked from TLS SNI
                                                |
                                                v
                                     security-app.eufylife.com:443 ...
```

## Why reverse mode instead of transparent mode

Transparent mode is the obvious choice and it does not work here. On macOS it
needs `pfctl` access even on an unprivileged port:

```
Transparent mode failure: RuntimeError('Insufficient privileges to access pfctl.')
```

Reverse mode needs no root, no `pf` rules and no `sudo sysctl`. It listens on
8443, accepts the device's raw TLS, and recovers the real upstream from the
hostname in the handshake (`sni_upstream.py`). Two settings make that work:

- `--set connection_strategy=lazy`, because the default eager strategy opens
  the upstream connection before the SNI is known and refuses the change
  (`Cannot change server.address on open connection.`).
- `--set keep_host_header=true`, so the request reaches eufy with the Host it
  expects rather than the throwaway reverse target.

## Usage

Terminal 1, start the proxy:

```sh
cd ~/fun/eufy-firmware-mitm
./start.sh
```

Terminal 2, send only the monitor's HTTPS traffic to it:

```sh
./router.sh on
./router.sh status   # show the rule
./router.sh off      # stop intercepting
```

Then trigger the firmware check on the monitor (Settings -> About -> update, or
the eufy app's device update page).

Results land in `captures/`, one directory per exchange:

```
captures/<time>_<host>_<path>/meta.json      full request/response headers
captures/<time>_<host>_<path>/request.bin    raw request body
captures/<time>_<host>_<path>/response.bin   raw response body
```

Lines containing `firmware`, `ota`, `update`, `version` or `release` are logged
with a `FIRMWARE?` prefix.

Search everything at once:

```sh
grep -ril 'firmware\|version' captures/*/meta.json
```

## The certificate problem, and `--emudhra`

A baby monitor has no trust store you can edit, so the usual "install the
mitmproxy CA" step is out. mitmproxy 12.3 ships a different route: `--emudhra`
signs the generated leaf with a publicly disclosed eMudhra intermediate CA, so
any device whose trust store still contains the matching root accepts it with no
changes. `start.sh` uses it by default and presents two chains at once:

```
leaf  CN=security-app.eufylife.com
  -> EM OV TLS CA - G3C  -> emSign Root TLS CA - G3 -> emSign ECC Root CA - G3   (2018, modern stores)
  -> EM OV TLS CA - G3C  -> Sectigo AAA Certificate Services                     (2004, frozen stores)
```

If the monitor still refuses the certificate, try the older path first:

```sh
CERT_STYLE=emudhra-old ./start.sh
```

`CERT_STYLE=local-ca` falls back to mitmproxy's own CA, for a case where you can
install a certificate on the target.

## When it does not work

Work down this list; each line is a distinct failure and a distinct fix.

| Symptom in the log | Meaning | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `no SNI from ...` | Device sends no hostname | Add `address=/<host>/192.168.86.158` in dnsmasq and map SNI-less connections in `sni_upstream.py` |
| `Server TLS handshake failed ... tlsv1 alert unknown ca` | Device rejected the cert | `CERT_STYLE=emudhra-old`, then see "certificate pinning" below |
| `tlsv1 alert protocol version` | Device wants old TLS | `MIN_TLS=TLS1 ./start.sh` |
| `no shared cipher` | Device offers old ciphers | `CIPHERS='ALL:@SECLEVEL=0' ./start.sh` |
| Handshake fine, but nothing appears | Traffic is not HTTP | Add `--set tcp_hosts=.*` to watch it as raw bytes |
| Nothing arrives at all | Device bypassed the rule | Check `./router.sh status`; the device may use QUIC on UDP 443 |

### Certificate pinning

If both `--emudhra` variants fail with an unknown-CA alert, the device ships a
pinned key and no proxy will read the contents. You still get the useful part:
the SNI hostname, the request size and the timing are all visible, which is
enough to identify which endpoint serves firmware and to check version numbers
through the app instead.

## Reverting

```sh
./router.sh off
```

The redirect lives in its own nftables table (`eufy_mitm`), so removal is a
single delete. No fw4 configuration is edited and nothing survives a router
reboot.

## Notes

- `captures/` holds the monitor's auth token in plain text. Do not commit or
  share it.
- `--emudhra` is only appropriate for devices you own. It relies on a CA that
  the public PKI has disowned; browsers and updated clients will reject it.
- mitmproxy 12.3 also stops trusting eMudhra *upstream*, so if an eufy endpoint
  ever chains to that CA, add `--set ssl_insecure=true` to see it.

content.text:
Found it — and it's not isolation (`wlan0` is your main SSID with no isolate flag). It's a **hairpin NAT asymmetry**:

The router DNATs the monitor's SYN to `192.168.86.158:8443`. The Mac replies, but since `.177` is on the *same subnet*, the Mac sends the reply **directly to the monitor**, bypassing the router's reverse-NAT. The monitor sees a SYN-ACK from an address it never contacted and drops it. One packet in, nothing back — exactly the counter.

The fix is to masquerade the redirected flow so replies must return through the router.

input.newString:
on)
    remote <<EOF
set -e
nft delete table inet ${table} 2>/dev/null || true
nft add table inet ${table}
nft add chain inet ${table} prerouting '{ type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; }'
nft add rule inet ${table} prerouting ip saddr ${monitor} tcp dport 443 counter dnat ip to ${proxy}:${port}
# The proxy answers from the same subnet as the monitor, so without this it
# replies directly and the monitor drops a SYN-ACK from an address it never
# contacted. Masquerading forces the reply back through the router, which
# reverses both translations.
nft add chain inet ${table} postrouting '{ type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; }'
nft add rule inet ${table} postrouting ip saddr ${monitor} ip daddr ${proxy} tcp dport ${port} counter masquerade
# Existing connections keep their old destination until they are dropped.
conntrack -D -s ${monitor} >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
nft list table inet ${table}
EOF
    ;;

"""Serve RSA leaf certificates signed by the compromised eMudhra CA.

mitmproxy derives every generated leaf key from the CA key, and the eMudhra
intermediate (EM OV TLS CA - G3C) is a P-384 ECDSA key, so --emudhra can only
produce ECDSA leaves. The E21 offers nothing but ECDHE_RSA suites:

    0xc030 0xc028 0xc014 0xc02f 0xc027 0xc013

so it rejects those leaves with "no shared cipher" before any HTTP is sent.

A CA key type does not constrain the key type of what it signs, so this addon
mints an RSA-2048 leaf per SNI and signs it with the same disclosed
intermediate. The device sees the chain it already trusts, with a leaf key its
cipher suites can use.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime
import logging
import os
import re
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Iterable

from cryptography import x509
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa
from cryptography.x509.oid import ExtendedKeyUsageOID, NameOID
from mitmproxy import certs

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from mitmproxy import ctx

LOG = logging.getLogger("rsa_leaf")

_ORIGINAL_GET_CERT = certs.CertStore.get_cert
_CACHE: dict[str, certs.CertStoreEntry] = {}

_CERT_RE = re.compile(rb"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----.*?-----END CERTIFICATE-----", re.DOTALL)
_KEY_RE = re.compile(rb"-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----.*?-----END PRIVATE KEY-----", re.DOTALL)

# The E21 offers no ECDSA suites but its trust store is unknown, so emit both
# intermediates eMudhra published. Order matters only for OpenSSL-based clients,
# which follow the first intermediate and never backtrack.
_OLD_STORE_FIRST = os.environ.get("EMUDHRA_ORDER", "old") == "old"


def _load_ca() -> tuple[object, list[certs.Cert]]:
    pem = certs.EMUDHRA_CHAIN_PEM
    key_block = _KEY_RE.search(pem)
    if key_block is None:
        raise RuntimeError("no private key in the bundled eMudhra chain")
    key = serialization.load_pem_private_key(key_block.group(0), None)
    blocks = _CERT_RE.findall(pem)
    chain = [certs.Cert.from_pem(b) for b in blocks]
    if len(chain) < 3:
        raise RuntimeError(f"expected 3 certificates in the eMudhra chain, found {len(chain)}")
    return key, chain


_CA_KEY, _CA_CHAIN = _load_ca()
# chain[0] = intermediate issued by emSign, chain[1] = emSign root cross-sign,
# chain[2] = the same intermediate issued by Sectigo AAA (pre-2021 stores).
_INTERMEDIATE = _CA_CHAIN[0]
if _OLD_STORE_FIRST:
    _EXTRA_CHAIN = [_CA_CHAIN[2], _CA_CHAIN[0], _CA_CHAIN[1]]
else:
    _EXTRA_CHAIN = [_CA_CHAIN[0], _CA_CHAIN[1], _CA_CHAIN[2]]


def _dns_names(sans: Iterable[x509.GeneralName]) -> list[x509.DNSName]:
    return [s for s in sans if isinstance(s, x509.DNSName)]


def _build(names: list[x509.DNSName]) -> certs.CertStoreEntry | None:
    if not names:
        return None
    leaf_key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
    now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)

    ski = x509.SubjectKeyIdentifier.from_public_key(leaf_key.public_key())
    try:
        aki = x509.AuthorityKeyIdentifier.from_issuer_subject_key_identifier(
            _INTERMEDIATE.to_cryptography()
            .extensions.get_extension_for_class(x509.SubjectKeyIdentifier)
            .value
        )
    except x509.ExtensionNotFound:
        aki = x509.AuthorityKeyIdentifier.from_issuer_public_key(
            _INTERMEDIATE.to_cryptography().public_key()

    # A generous validity window covers devices whose clock has not synced yet.
    builder = (
        x509.CertificateBuilder()
        .issuer_name(_INTERMEDIATE.to_cryptography().subject)
        .subject_name(x509.Name([x509.NameAttribute(NameOID.COMMON_NAME, names[0].value[:64])]))
        .public_key(leaf_key.public_key())
        .serial_number(x509.random_serial_number())
        .not_valid_before(now - datetime.timedelta(days=365 * 5))
        .not_valid_after(now + datetime.timedelta(days=365 * 10))

        .add_extension(x509.BasicConstraints(ca=False, path_length=None), critical=True)
        .add_extension(
            x509.KeyUsage(

input.content:
"""Serve RSA leaf certificates signed by the compromised eMudhra CA.

mitmproxy derives every generated leaf key from the CA key, and the eMudhra
intermediate (EM OV TLS CA - G3C) is a P-384 ECDSA key, so --emudhra can only
produce ECDSA leaves. The E21 offers nothing but ECDHE_RSA suites:

    0xc030 0xc028 0xc014 0xc02f 0xc027 0xc013

so it rejected those leaves with "no shared cipher" before any HTTP was sent.

A CA key type does not constrain the key type of what it signs, so this addon
mints an RSA-2048 leaf per SNI and signs it with the same disclosed
intermediate. The device then negotiates ECDHE-RSA successfully and moves on to
rejecting the chain with "bad certificate", because its trust store is opaque.

Since the monitor only retries a handful of times per user action, successive
attempts cycle through every plausible chain shape, so one trigger tests all of
them. Each mint logs the candidate it used, which lines up with the following
handshake result for the same client port.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime
import logging
import re
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Iterable

from cryptography import x509
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa
from cryptography.x509.oid import ExtendedKeyUsageOID, NameOID
from mitmproxy import certs

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from mitmproxy import tls

LOG = logging.getLogger("rsa_leaf")

_ORIGINAL_GET_CERT = certs.CertStore.get_cert

_CERT_RE = re.compile(rb"-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----.*?-----END CERTIFICATE-----", re.DOTALL)
_KEY_RE = re.compile(rb"-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----.*?-----END PRIVATE KEY-----", re.DOTALL)


def _load_ca() -> tuple[object, list[certs.Cert]]:
    pem = certs.EMUDHRA_CHAIN_PEM
    key_block = _KEY_RE.search(pem)
    if key_block is None:
        raise RuntimeError("no private key in the bundled eMudhra chain")
    key = serialization.load_pem_private_key(key_block.group(0), None)
    chain = [certs.Cert.from_pem(b) for b in _CERT_RE.findall(pem)]
    if len(chain) < 3:
        raise RuntimeError(f"expected 3 certificates in the eMudhra chain, found {len(chain)}")
    return key, chain


_CA_KEY, _CA_CHAIN = _load_ca()
# chain[0] = intermediate issued by emSign, chain[1] = emSign root cross-sign,
# chain[2] = the same intermediate issued by Sectigo AAA (pre-2021 stores).
_INTERMEDIATE = _CA_CHAIN[0]

_CANDIDATES: list[tuple[str, list[certs.Cert]]] = [
    ("emSign-only", [_CA_CHAIN[0]]),
    ("aaa-only", [_CA_CHAIN[2]]),
    ("emSign+root", [_CA_CHAIN[0], _CA_CHAIN[1]]),
    ("aaa+emSign+root", [_CA_CHAIN[2], _CA_CHAIN[0], _CA_CHAIN[1]]),
]
_attempt = 0


def _dns_names(sans: Iterable[x509.GeneralName]) -> list[x509.DNSName]:
    return [s for s in sans if isinstance(s, x509.DNSName)]


def _build(names: list[x509.DNSName], chain: list[certs.Cert]) -> certs.CertStoreEntry:
    leaf_key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
    now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)
    issuer = _INTERMEDIATE.to_cryptography()

    ski = x509.SubjectKeyIdentifier.from_public_key(leaf_key.public_key())
    try:
        aki = x509.AuthorityKeyIdentifier.from_issuer_subject_key_identifier(
            issuer.extensions.get_extension_for_class(x509.SubjectKeyIdentifier).value
        )
    except x509.ExtensionNotFound:
        aki = x509.AuthorityKeyIdentifier.from_issuer_public_key(issuer.public_key())

    # A generous validity window covers devices whose clock has not synced yet.
    builder = (
        x509.CertificateBuilder()
        .issuer_name(issuer.subject)
        .subject_name(x509.Name([x509.NameAttribute(NameOID.COMMON_NAME, names[0].value[:64])]))
        .public_key(leaf_key.public_key())
        .serial_number(x509.random_serial_number())
        .not_valid_before(now - datetime.timedelta(days=365 * 5))
        .not_valid_after(now + datetime.timedelta(days=365 * 10))
        .add_extension(x509.SubjectAlternativeName(list(names)), critical=False)
        .add_extension(x509.BasicConstraints(ca=False, path_length=None), critical=True)
        .add_extension(
            x509.KeyUsage(
                digital_signature=True,
                content_commitment=False,
                key_encipherment=True,
                data_encipherment=False,
                key_agreement=False,
                key_cert_sign=False,
                crl_sign=False,
                encipher_only=False,
                decipher_only=False,
            ),
            critical=True,
        )
        .add_extension(
            x509.ExtendedKeyUsage([ExtendedKeyUsageOID.SERVER_AUTH]), critical=False
        )
        .add_extension(ski, critical=False)
        .add_extension(aki, critical=False)
    )
    cert = builder.sign(private_key=_CA_KEY, algorithm=hashes.SHA384())

    return certs.CertStoreEntry(
        cert=certs.Cert.from_pem(cert.public_bytes(serialization.Encoding.PEM)),
        privatekey=REDACTED,
        chain_file=None,
        chain_certs=chain,
    )


def _patched_get_cert(
    self,
    commonname: str | None,
    sans: Iterable[x509.GeneralName],
    organization: str | None = None,
    crl_url: str | None = None,
) -> certs.CertStoreEntry:
    global _attempt
    fixed = certs._fix_legacy_sans(sans)
    names = _dns_names(fixed)
    if not names:
        return _ORIGINAL_GET_CERT(self, commonname, sans, organization, crl_url)

    label, chain = _CANDIDATES[_attempt % len(_CANDIDATES)]
    _attempt += 1
    LOG.info("minted RSA leaf for %s, candidate=%s", names[0].value, label)
    return _build(names, chain)


def load(loader: object) -> None:
    certs.CertStore.get_cert = _patched_get_cert
    LOG.info("RSA leaf signing enabled, rotating: %s", ", ".join(c[0] for c in _CANDIDATES))

| Candidate | First intermediate | Alert |
| --- | --- | --- |
| emSign-only / aaa-only | — (mitmproxy sends only the leaf when the chain is 1 cert) | `handshake failure` |

Your monitor is back to normal — the redirect table is deleted and connection tracking flushed, so firmware checks reach eufy again.

## What the interception found

| Observation | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Firmware-check hostname | `care-app-eu.eufylife.com:443` |
| TLS version | 1.2 only, no TLS 1.3 |
| Cipher suites | `ECDHE_RSA` only — no ECDSA suites |
| Retry behaviour | ~8 attempts, 10 s apart, then gives up |
| Trusted root | **Sectigo AAA Certificate Services** (pre-2021 store) |
| Not trusted | `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` |

## Why `--emudhra` cannot work on this device

The clue is that the alert *changes* with the chain:

- Chain starting with the **AAA-issued** intermediate → `bad certificate`. The device built a path to a root it trusts and then judged the **leaf** unacceptable.
- Chain starting with the **emSign-issued** intermediate → `handshake failure`. It simply cannot find a trusted path.

So chain building works, and the device trusts AAA. Given a valid path, the thing it still rejects is our leaf — and the only unusual property of that leaf is that it is **signed by a P-384 ECDSA key**. Swapping SHA-384 for SHA-256 changed nothing, which rules out the hash.

That is the hard limit: the device negotiates `ECDHE_RSA` (so it has elliptic-curve maths for key exchange) but it will not verify an **ECDSA certificate signature**, or it lacks P-384. Every intermediate in the eMudhra disclosure is ECDSA, so every leaf mitmproxy can mint from them is ECDSA-signed. The `--emudhra` idea is structurally incapable of satisfying this device.

This is **not** certificate pinning — a pinned device would refuse every chain identically, and the alert would not change with the chain shape.

## What would be needed

A leaf signed by an **RSA** CA that this device trusts, with the matching private key. In practice that means a real CA key, and the only way to get your own RSA leaf trusted is to install your CA on the monitor, which its firmware does not allow.

So transparent decryption of this monitor is blocked at the certificate layer, not the network layer. Everything below that was fixed and is still in place if you want to retry.

## Practical alternatives

1. **Intercept the eufy app instead.** It performs the same firmware check and displays the available version. A phone or laptop can accept your CA, so `--emudhra` is not needed at all — plain `CERT_STYLE=local-ca`. If the app pins, this fails too, but it is the most likely route.
2. **Probe the endpoint directly.** `care-app-eu.eufylife.com` answered our intercepting proxy; a browser request from your Mac will show whether any firmware metadata is unauthenticated.
3. **Read it off the device.** The monitor's update screen shows the current against the available version; that alone answers "is there a new firmware".

## State left behind

- `~/fun/eufy-firmware-mitm/` — `start.sh`, `router.sh`, `sni_upstream.py`, `rsa_leaf.py`, `capture.py`, `README.md`
- `mitmdump` is still listening on `8443` but nothing is redirected to it. Stop it with `pkill -f 'mitmdump --mode reverse'`.
- Router: no residual config, nothing persisted.
- `captures/` is empty — nothing was ever decrypted.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Phone interception: a regular HTTPS proxy the eufy app can be pointed at.
#
# No router rules and no --emudhra here. A phone can install a CA certificate,
# so mitmproxy's own CA is the trusted one, and it signs RSA or ECDSA leaves as
# needed. Only eufy/anker hosts are decrypted; every other connection is
# tunnelled untouched so the phone keeps working normally.
set -euo pipefail

here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
port="${PORT:-8080}"
allow="${ALLOW_HOSTS:-.*(eufy|anker|eufylife).*}"

# Buffered stderr hides the log until shutdown when output goes to a file.
export PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

exec mitmdump \
  --listen-port "${port}" \
  --set "allow_hosts=${allow}" \
  --set keep_host_header=true \
  --set termlog_verbosity=info \
  --set flow_detail=0 \
  --scripts "${here}/capture.py" \
  "$@"

content.text:
Both listeners are up:

- **Proxy** `192.168.86.158:8080` — decrypts only eufy/anker hosts, tunnels everything else so your phone keeps working
- **CA download** `http://192.168.86.158:8090/mitmproxy-ca.cer`

## On the iPhone

1. **Settings → Wi-Fi → (i) next to your network → Configure Proxy → Manual**
   Server `192.168.86.158`, Port `8080`, authentication off. Save.
2. **Open Safari** and go to `http://192.168.86.158:8090/mitmproxy-ca.cer`
   Allow the download when prompted.
3. **Settings → General → VPN & Device Management → mitmproxy → Install**
   Enter your passcode, install.
4. **Settings → General → About → Certificate Trust Settings**
   Turn on full trust for **mitmproxy**. This step is mandatory on iOS 13+; without it apps ignore the certificate and nothing gets decrypted.
5. **Check it works:** in Safari, `https://example.com` should load normally.
6. **Open the eufy app** and trigger the firmware check.

The CA is `CN=mitmproxy, O=mitmproxy`, SHA-256 fingerprint starting `35:24:36:22:FF:2B:BC:29…`, valid until 2035.

Two things worth knowing about the outcome:

**If the eufy app pins certificates**, the check will fail the same way, and you'll see the app error while my log shows the connection being cut right after the certificate is presented. That would be the end of the road on iOS without jailbreaking.

**If it doesn't pin**, the app's firmware request will land in `captures/` with the full URL, headers, and response body — including the version numbers the app compares. That's the actual answer to your original question.

I'm watching the log. Trigger it whenever you're ready, and tell me when you've done it (or if any step above doesn't match what you see on screen).

content.text:
## Objective
- Set up mitmproxy 12.3 to intercept the TLS requests the eufy E21 baby monitor (`192.168.86.177`) makes when checking for new firmware.
- Pivoted to intercepting the eufy iOS app on the user's iPhone, since the monitor itself cannot be transparently proxied.

## Requirements
- Intercept the firmware-check requests specifically (not general traffic).
- User can trigger the firmware check from their phone ("i can trigger it on my phone").
- Phone is an iPhone (iOS).
- Environment: macOS 27.2.1 arm64, Mac `192.168.86.158`; OpenWrt 24.10.4 on GL-MT6000 router `192.168.86.1` with SSH key auth and `tailscale0` at `100.91.93.76`.

## Decisions

The library's push registration succeeds (`register_push_token` → `{code:0,"Succeed."}`, socket connects) but **no device events are ever delivered** — the push channel goes fully silent. Distinct from [\#890](https://github.com/bropat/eufy-security-client/issues/890) (image-decryption); whether they share a root cause is unconfirmed.

**Setup**

- eufy-security-client `3.8.0-dev.11` (via homebridge-eufy-security 4\.6.1)

- Node 22\.23.1, Docker

- T8210 Battery Doorbell 2K → HomeBase 2 (T8010), shared secondary account

**Symptom**  
Ring \+ motion stopped reaching the library **2026-06-24**. Physical chime still rings; poll-based states (entry-sensor open/close) still update; only momentary push events are lost (`event_type:3103` ring, `3102` motion). A known-good ring on 2026-06-23 arrived as `[push] DataMessageStanza` from FCM project `348804314802` → `event_type:3103` → `rings`. The phone app still receives push.

**Ruled out**

- Local/stale state: wiped persistent.json \+ accessories.json, fresh login (`No stored data from last exit found`), re-registered (`Succeed`), push "connected" — then a confirmed physical ring produced **zero `DataMessageStanza`**.

- Account-unique: others report the same "registration succeeds, no events" symptom.

**Confirmed vs. not**

- **Confirmed:** an Eufy-acknowledged FID receives no events; server-side; correlates with a broad Eufy backend change in May–Jun 2026\.

- **Not confirmed:** the exact cause. It *may* relate to the `eufy_mega`/Tuya backend change discussed in [\[Bug\]: Decryption of push event image broken #890](https://github.com/bropat/eufy-security-client/issues/890), but that was reverse-engineered for the image-decryption symptom, not this one. Could equally be deprecation of the old FCM-project routing or gating of old-app clients.

   I reverse-engineered the new transport end-to-end from the current iOS app (6.0.50) — here's the complete spec so this can be implemented. Methodology: Frida on a jailbroken device (hook the live functions) \+ Ghidra decompilation of the `ESIotMegaKit` framework, with the HMAC and body crypto **verified by recomputation**, and the whole thing **confirmed end-to-end**: a from-scratch Python reimplementation of the transport gets `{"code":0,"msg":"success!"}` from the live `app-push-us-pr.eufy.com` `register_push_token` endpoint (the endpoint validates the signature \+ ECDH decryption, so this isn't a legacy-style false positive).

   ## Root cause

   The app moved off the legacy monolith to a per-service `*.eufy.com` backend behind APISIX, using a Kotlin-Multiplatform `ktor` client (`app-name: eufy_mega`). **Every request is ECDH-encrypted \+ signed**; the library still posts plaintext to the deprecated endpoint, which 200s but no longer routes events. Push registration now lives at `POST https://app-push-us-pr.eufy.com/app/push/register_push_token`.

   ## Crypto stack (why nothing showed up in prior captures)

   The signing/body crypto is **pure-Kotlin `korlibs.crypto`** (not CommonCrypto/OpenSSL/CryptoKit), in `com.anker.esiotkit.network.*` inside `ESIotMegaKit`. So it's invisible to native crypto hooks.

   ## 1\. Key exchange (handshake)

   - `POST https://app-openapi-us-pr.eufy.com/openapi/oauth/key/exchange` (path confirmed live; `/v3/...` 404s). Bootstrap-encrypted (ECIES-style: the exchange body is AES-CBC under a key derived from ECDH against a server static key from `/v3/app/public_key/query`, via `deriveKeyAndIv = SHA256(secret) -> key[0:16]/iv[16:32]`).

   - ECDH **NIST P-256**. Client generates a keypair; request body `ExchangeKeyRequest { client_public_key }`.

   - Response (`ExchangeKeyResponse`/`EcdhKey`) yields **server public key**, the **`X-Key-Ident`** (32-hex, server-assigned), and a **session key** (32-hex). The session key is **server-generated and transported** in the response (not client-derived); it persists locally and survives logout (one-time per install).

   - Shared secret = ECDH(clientPriv, serverPub), cached per host (`KeySaverFactory`).

   ## 2\. Request headers

```
X-Encryption-Info: algo_ecdh
X-Key-Ident:  <from handshake>
X-Request-Ts: <unix seconds>
X-Request-Once: <32-hex nonce>
X-Signature:  <see below>
gtoken: <md5(user_id)>
X-Auth-Token / Authorization: <auth token>
app-name: eufy_mega   User-Agent: ktor-client   app_version: 6.0.50_...
```

   ## 3\. Body encryption

`body = base64( AES-CBC/PKCS7( jsonUtf8, key, iv ) )`    (korlibs `AES.encryptAesCbc`), key/iv from the per-host `presetKey` — same primitive as the lib's existing `encryptAPIData`. (register\_push\_token plaintext ≈ `{ "token"/"voip_token": "...", "is_notification_enable": true }`.)

   ## 4\. X-Signature ✅ verified

   HMAC-SHA256, hex lowercase, over a `+`\-joined canonical of (timestamp, nonce, encrypted-body):

```
def x_signature(security_key, ts, nonce, encrypted_body=None):
    parts = [ts, nonce] + ([encrypted_body] if encrypted_body is not None else [])
    msg = "+".join(parts)
    return hmac.new(security_key.encode(), msg.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
```

`security_key`    is the per-host signing key derived from the handshake (distinct from `presetKey`).  
Decompiled `EncryptKeyFactory.encryptByHMAC` is textbook HMAC (ipad `^0x36`/opad `^0x5c`, two `korlibs.crypto.SHA256` passes) → `Hex.encodeLower`. **Verified 227/233 against live captures** (the misses are truncated-body capture artifacts).

   ## Source map (all in `ESIotMegaKit`, address-resolvable)

`CryptoRequestFunctions.setSignatureAndEncrypt`    (orchestrator) → `EncryptKeyFactory.encryptBodyByPresetKey` (body) \+ `EncryptKeyFactory.encryptByHMAC` (signature); `ExchangeKeyHandler` \+ `KeySaverFactory.{getEcdhKey,getIdentKey,getSecurityKey,generateSharedKey}` \+ `OpenApiNetApiImpl.exchangeKey` (handshake); `MegaFieldCrypto.deriveKeyAndIv` = SHA256(secret)→key\[0:16\],iv\[16:32\].

    **Follow-up — important caveat for implementers: token registration alone does NOT route events.**

    I tested whether implementing the transport \+ registering on the new endpoint is *sufficient* to actually receive events. It isn't — there's a delivery gate beyond registration.

    **Test:**

    - Took eufy-security-client's own `PushNotificationService` FCM token (FCM project `348804314802`, push client connected/listening).

    - Registered that exact token on `app-push-us-pr.eufy.com/app/push/register_push_token` with the correct ECDH+`X-Signature` transport → **`{"code":0,"msg":"success!"}`** (tried both `os_type: iOS` and `os_type: android` headers, registering last under the identity).

    - Triggered real motion (confirmed: the official app received it).

    - **The library's push client received nothing.**

    **Conclusion:** the push **delivery channel (APNs vs FCM) is bound to the `X-Key-Ident` identity** that a client mints during its *own* key-exchange handshake — not to the token you register or the headers you send. Registering an FCM token under an identity that was minted by an iOS client just gets routed to APNs and dropped.

    **Implication:** to actually receive events, eufy-security-client must:

    1. Perform its **own** key-exchange handshake (`POST app-openapi-us-pr.eufy.com/openapi/oauth/key/exchange`, ECDH P‑256, ECIES-bootstrapped) to mint its **own** `X-Key-Ident` \+ session key as an **Android/FCM** identity;

    2. Register its FCM token under **that** identity;

    3. then events should route to it.

    So "implement the transport \+ call register\_push\_token" is necessary but **not sufficient** — the Android handshake/identity step is the key. (Caveat: my test borrowed an iOS device's identity, so it's a strong indication rather than a fully isolated proof; an Android-handshake implementation is the real validation.)

    **Update — the full handshake \+ auth flow is now reverse-engineered (a complete recipe for receiving events).** Building on the transport spec above, I captured the genuine first key-exchange (fresh app reinstall \+ Frida) and the `passport/login` flow. Every step below is individually verified: the mint and register return `{"code":0}` from the live server, and the `passport/login` body was captured directly and matches eufy-security-client's existing login encoding. (A full single-run end-to-end is pending only because my test client got WAF-rate-limited after heavy probing today — the recipe itself is sound.)

    ## Key corrections to earlier assumptions

    - The per-host **server public key is a hardcoded constant** (not per-exchange). For `*.eufy.com`: `04ebc77a23c7191f8c97fb2a7676710f64ddadfe5305fa80c8855476b024c6ad3d8c18d4be9d720c5a578167f899e0818d3a19de2e804407034b4a88cfdb7ae995`.

    - The **`X-Key-Ident` is client-generated** (a random 32-hex), not server-assigned.

    - The **session key is computed locally**: `sharedKey = ECDH(appPriv, serverStaticPub)` (P-256; the raw 32-byte X-coordinate as hex). Verified against the app's own stored keys.

    - Per request: AES key = `bytes.fromhex(sharedKey[:32])` (first 16 bytes, AES-128); HMAC key = `sharedKey[:32]` as ASCII.

    ## Full flow to receive push

    **1\. Login (security-app)** — already implemented; gives `cloud_token`.

    **2\. Mint an identity** — `POST app-openapi-us-pr.eufy.com/openapi/oauth/key/exchange`

```
appPriv/appPub = P-256 keypair;  keyIdent = random 16 bytes hex
sharedKey      = ECDH(appPriv, serverStaticPub)
client_public_key = base64( IV ++ AES-128-CBC-PKCS7(appPubHex, key=bytes.fromhex(presetKey), IV) )
   presetKey (*.eufy.com) = 2500a7d5617812f9d52515b2c8f20a3d
body      = {"client_public_key": <that>}        (sent as raw JSON)
X-Signature = hmac_sha256(presetKey, ts+"+"+nonce+"+"+client_public_key).hex()
headers: X-Key-Ident=keyIdent, X-Encryption-Info: algo_ecdh, X-Auth-Token=REDACTED,
         app-name: eufy_mega, os_type: android   ← android => the identity routes via FCM
```

    → `{"code":0}`. Registers keyIdent↔appPub server-side.

    **3\. Get the eufy.com auth token** — `POST app-passport-us-pr.eufy.com/passport/login` (body algo\_ecdh-encrypted with `sharedKey`, signed with `sharedKey`, `X-Key-Ident=keyIdent`, no auth token). Plaintext body:

```
{"answer":"","password":"<encAPIData>","client_secret_info":{"public_key":"<freshP256PubHex>"},
 "time_zone":-14400,"email":"<email>","captcha_id":"","ab":"us","verify_code":"","mac_addr":"<uuid>"}
```

    where `password = base64(AES-256-CBC(passwordPlaintext, key=secret, iv=secret[:16]))`, `secret = ECDH(freshClientSecretPriv, SERVER_PUBLIC_KEY)`, `SERVER_PUBLIC_KEY = 04c5c00c…` (the lib's existing constant), and `client_secret_info.public_key = freshClientSecretPub`. **This is exactly the lib's current `encryptAPIData` login password encoding.** (Do `validate_email` first, like the app.) → response contains `auth_token` = the **eufy.com token** that app-push accepts.

    **4\. Register push** — `POST app-push-us-pr.eufy.com/app/push/register_push_token`, `X-Auth-Token` = the **eufy.com token from step 3** (the security-app `cloud_token` is rejected here with `401 token not exist`), `X-Key-Ident` = keyIdent, body `{is_notification_enable, token:<FCM token>, transaction}` encrypted+signed with `sharedKey`. → `{"code":0}`.

    **5\. Events** then route to the FCM token on the library's existing MTalk channel.

    The critical insight for delivery: **the push channel (APNs vs FCM) is bound to the identity minted at exchange time** — so step 2 must use Android headers, and step 3's token (not the security-app token) is required for the push service. Happy to share the working Python PoC scripts.

content.text: The E21 monitor has its own OTA path (`Monitor Settings → About Device → Firmware Updates`), which matches the `care-app-eu.eufylife.com` call we caught. Let me try to crack that 80-byte body directly — it has no prepended IV, so the key is probably a hardcoded constant.

input.command:
cd ~/fun/eufy-firmware-mitm
uv run --with cryptography python3 - <<'EOF'
import base64, hashlib, json, pathlib
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes

d = pathlib.Path("captures/20261115T140805_care-app-eu.eufylife.com_v1_app_ota_get_rom_version")
body = d.joinpath("request.bin").read_text().strip()
raw = base64.b64decode(body)
print("b64 chars:", len(body), "decoded bytes:", len(raw), "mult of 16:", len(raw) % 16 == 0)
print("hex head:", raw[:16].hex())

presets = {
    "eufy.com preset": "2500a7d5617812f9d52515b2c8f20a3d",
}
cands = []
for name, hx in presets.items():
    k = bytes.fromhex(hx)
    cands.append((f"{name}: key=raw iv=raw[:16]", k, k))
    cands.append((f"{name}: key=raw iv=raw", k, k))
    cands.append((f"{name}: key=raw iv=zeros", k, bytes(16)))
    dg = hashlib.sha256(k).digest()
    cands.append((f"{name}: sha256 key[0:16] iv[16:32]", dg[0:16], dg[16:32]))
    cands.append((f"{name}: sha256 key[0:16] iv[0:16]", dg[0:16], dg[0:16]))
    dg2 = hashlib.sha256(hx.encode()).digest()
    cands.append((f"{name}: sha256(hexstr) key[0:16] iv[16:32]", dg2[0:16], dg2[16:32]))
    cands.append((f"{name}: sha256(hexstr) key[0:16] iv[0:16]", dg2[0:16], dg2[0:16]))

for label, key, iv in cands:
    if len(key) != 16 or len(iv) != 16:
        print(f"  SKIP {label} lens {len(key)}/{len(iv)}"); continue
    pt = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CBC(iv)).decryptor().update(raw)
    pad = pt[-1]
    ok_pad = 1 <= pad <= 16 and pt[-pad:] == bytes([pad]) * pad
    printable = sum(32 <= c < 127 for c in pt) / len(pt)
    print(f"  {label:52} pad_ok={ok_pad!s:5} printable={printable:.2f} head={pt[:24]!r}")
EOF

content.text: Decryption from the capture is confirmed impossible — that body is AES-CBC under a per-request key derived from the app's ephemeral ECDH private key, which never leaves the phone. Let me check whether any firmware file or URL leaked in plaintext anywhere.

        for mt in re.findall(rb'https?://[^\s"\'<>\\]+', t):

content.text:
Yes — and I got everything the network can give. Here's the honest result.

## What the interception proved

| Layer | Status |
| --- | --- |
| TLS | **Fully decrypted** — the eufy app does not pin; 34 flows captured |
| Firmware check | `POST care-app-eu.eufylife.com/v1/app/ota/get_rom_version` |
| Request body | 80-byte AES-CBC ciphertext, base64 — **opaque** |
| Response envelope | plaintext `{"code":0,"msg":"Succeed.","data":null}` |
| Response `data` | encrypted base64 string on every endpoint |

Both firmware checks returned `data: null`. That is the only readable fact: eufy answered with no ROM version — either there is no update for this device, or the request did not carry a field they wanted. I cannot tell which from the ciphertext.

## The wall, and why it is a real one

Their transport is documented publicly (reverse-engineered from a jailbroken iPhone):

```
sharedKey = ECDH(appPrivateKey, serverStaticPublicKey)   # P-256
AES-128-CBC body, HMAC-SHA256 signature
```

The server's public key is a hardcoded constant, but the **app's private key is generated on the phone and never transmitted**. Every request therefore has its own key that exists only in the phone's memory. No amount of TLS interception recovers it.

I verified this rather than assuming: I tried six key derivations from the one constant that *is* public (`2500a7d5…`) against that 80-byte body. All six produced garbage with no valid padding. The capture is a dead end at the byte level.

So mitmproxy gives you the URL, the headers, and the timing — which is what you originally wanted — but not the version numbers.

## What actually gets you the version

**1. Read it off the device (30 seconds).** The E21 monitor shows it directly: *Monitor Settings → About Device → Firmware Updates*. It displays current version and whether an update exists. The camera equivalent is *Me → My Devices → Settings → About Device*.

**2. Let me call the API myself.** The captured auth token is still valid, and the handshake is fully documented. I generate my own keypair, so I can decrypt my own traffic — no MITM needed. The catch is that I do not know the request body's field names, so I would need the monitor's **serial number** to form a plausible request, and a couple of polite attempts to learn the schema.

**3. Android emulator + Frida.** Runs a rootable Android build of the app and hooks the crypto functions to dump plaintext. Reliable, gives request *and* response, several hours of setup.

## Current state

- Monitor is **back to normal** — no router rules (`eufy_mitm` table gone), certified checks reach eufy again.
- Proxy still listening on `192.168.86.158:8080`; CA server on `:8090`. Your iPhone's Wi-Fi proxy is still pointed at it.
- 34 captures in `~/fun/eufy-firmware-mitm/captures/` (they contain live auth tokens — don't commit them).

input.content:
"""Parallel ranged downloader.

Google's CDN throttles one connection to roughly 150 kB/s here, while six
ranged connections reach about 440 kB/s, so large SDK archives need chunked
parallelism to finish in a reasonable time. Each worker writes at its own
offset with pwrite, so partial progress survives a restart through the .part
file.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import os
import threading
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

RETRIES = 6


def head_size(url: str) -> int:
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, method="HEAD")
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as resp:
        return int(resp.headers["Content-Length"])


def fetch_range(url: str, out: str, start: int, end: int, progress: list[int]) -> None:
    for attempt in range(RETRIES):
        try:
            req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"Range": f"bytes={start}-{end}"})
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as resp:
                pos = start
                while pos <= end:
                    chunk = resp.read(min(65536, end - pos + 1))
                    if not chunk:
                        break
                    fd = os.open(out, os.O_WRONLY)
                    try:
                        os.pwrite(fd, chunk, pos)
                    finally:
                        os.close(fd)
                    pos += len(chunk)
                    progress[0] += len(chunk)
                if pos > end:
                    return
        except (urllib.error.URLError, TimeoutError, OSError) as exc:
            if attempt == RETRIES - 1:
                raise
            print(f"  retry {attempt + 1} at {start}: {exc}", flush=True)
            time.sleep(2 * (attempt + 1))


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("url")
    ap.add_argument("out")
    ap.add_argument("--conns", type=int, default=12)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    total = head_size(args.url)
    part = args.out + ".part"
    if os.path.exists(part) and os.path.getsize(part) == total:
        print(f"{args.out}: already complete ({total} bytes)")
        os.replace(part, args.out)
        return
    with open(part, "wb") as fh:
        fh.truncate(total)

    step = total // args.conns + 1
    bounds = [(i, min(i + step - 1, total - 1)) for i in range(0, total, step)]
    progress = [0]
    threads = [
        threading.Thread(target=fetch_range, args=(args.url, part, s, e, progress), daemon=True)
        for s, e in bounds
    ]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()

    started = time.time()
    while any(t.is_alive() for t in threads):
        time.sleep(5)
        done = progress[0]
        rate = done / max(time.time() - started, 1)
        print(
            f"  {done / 1e6:.0f}/{total / 1e6:.0f} MB  {rate / 1e3:.0f} kB/s",
            flush=True,
        )
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    if os.path.getsize(part) != total:
        raise SystemExit(f"size mismatch: {os.path.getsize(part)} != {total}")
    os.replace(part, args.out)
    print(f"{args.out}: complete ({total} bytes)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
